pll2d7c2-d1e3514.summary: Objects that since the good cannot sin and the bad cannot will well, they seem to lack free choice, which is open to both.

pll2d7c2-d1e3517.summary: Cites Jerome: only God cannot sin; all others, having free choice, can turn either way. So both good and bad angels could turn either way.

pll2d7c2-d1e3532.summary: Answers: the good are so confirmed by grace they cannot become evil, the bad so hardened they cannot become good; yet both have free choice, since the good choose good not by compelling necessity but by their own will, helped by grace, and the bad avoid good by their own will, deprived of grace. The bad have free choice, but depressed and corrupted so that it cannot rise to good.
claims: Both good and bad angels have free choice.
Choice by one's own will without coercion is free.
The bad angels' free choice is corrupted.

pl-l2d7c2.summary: Asks whether, since the good cannot sin and the bad cannot will well, they still have free choice, which is open to both; Jerome says every free creature can turn either way. Lombard answers that both have free choice: the good choose good not by necessity but by their own will, helped by grace; the bad avoid good and follow evil by their own will, deprived of grace; the bad have free choice, but depressed and corrupted so it cannot rise to good.
claims: Confirmed good angels cannot become evil; obstinate bad angels cannot become good.
Both still have free choice, acting by their own will, not necessity.
The good choose good with the help of grace.
The bad have free choice, but corrupted so that it cannot rise to good.
